blocks.md: What is a human but an ingenious machine designed to turn, with “infinite artfulness, the red wine of Shiraz into urine?” So said the storyteller in Isak Dinesen’s Seven Gothic Tales. More accurately but less poetically, human kidneys serve to convert more than 1700 L of blood per day into about 1 L of a highly concentrated fluid called urine. In so doing, the kidney excretes the waste products of metabolism; precisely regulates the body’s concentration of water, salt, calcium, phosphorus, and other anions and cations; and maintains the appropriate acid-base balance of plasma. The kidney also serves as an endocrine organ, secreting hormones such as erythropoietin and renin, and Renal diseases are responsible for a great deal of morbidity and mortality. According to the 2020 US Renal Data System Annual Data Report, more than 808,000 Americans had end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), of whom two-thirds are maintained on dialysis, at a cost of approximately $72,000 per person annually. The 1-year mortality rate of ESKD, when the enhanced risk for cardiovascular disease conferred by ESKD is considered, exceeds that of most newly diagnosed cancers.

**Acute kidney injury** occurs in more than 2 million people worldwide, and it is a major risk factor for the development of **chronic kidney disease** and ESKD. In addition, millions of people are affected annually by nonfatal kidney diseases, most notably infections of the kidney or lower urinary tract, kidney stones, and urinary obstruction. The availability of dialysis and the success of renal transplantation have improved the outlook for patients.

The study of kidney diseases is facilitated by categorizing them according to their primary effects on one of the four basic anatomic components of the kidney: glomeruli, tubules, interstitium, and blood vessels. This approach is useful because the early manifestations of disease primarily affecting one of these components tend to be distinct. Further, some components seem to be more vulnerable to specific forms of renal injury; for example, most glomerular diseases are immunologically mediated, whereas tubular and interstitial disorders are frequently caused by toxic or infectious agents. However, some disorders affect more than one structure, and the anatomic and functional interdependence of the components of the kidney means that damage to one usually secondarily affects the others. Primary disorders of the blood vessels, for example, inevitably affect all structures supplied by these vessels. Severe glomerular damage impairs the flow through the peritubular vascular system; conversely, tubular destruction, by increasing intraglomerular pressure, induces glomerular injury. Thus, whatever the origin, all forms of chronic kidney disease ultimately damage all four components of the kidney, culminating in what are called end-stage kidneys. The functional reserve of the kidney is large, and much damage may occur before there is evident functional impairment.
For these reasons, recognizing the early signs and symptoms is of high clinical importance.
CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF RENAL DISEASES

Azotemia is a biochemical abnormality that refers to an elevation of blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine levels, related largely to a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Azotemia is a consequence of many renal diseases, but it may also arise from extrarenal disorders. It is a typical feature of both acute and chronic kidney injury. Prerenal azotemia is encountered when there is hypoperfusion of the kidneys that impairs renal function in the absence of parenchymal damage. It may be caused by hypotension, excessive fluid losses from any cause, or if the effective intravascular volume is decreased due to shock or congestive **heart failure**. Postrenal azotemia is seen whenever urine flow is obstructed distal to the kidney. Relief of the obstruction is followed by correction of the azotemia.

When azotemia leads to clinical signs and symptoms associated with biochemical abnormalities, it is termed uremia. Uremia is characterized not only by failure of renal excretory function but also by a host of metabolic and endocrine alterations resulting from renal damage. Uremic patients frequently manifest secondary involvement of the gastrointestinal system (e.g., uremic gastroenteritis), peripheral nerves (e.g., peripheral neuropathy), and heart (e.g., uremic fibrinous **pericarditis**).

Nephritic syndrome is a clinical entity caused by inflammatory glomerular disease and is dominated by the acute onset of either grossly visible or microscopic hematuria, diminished GFR, mild to moderate proteinuria, and hypertension. It is the classic presentation of acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is a form of nephritic syndrome in which there is rapid decline in GFR (within hours to days).

Nephrotic syndrome, typically caused by severe dysfunction of the glomerular filter, is characterized by heavy proteinuria (more than 3.5 g/day), resulting in hypoalbuminemia and severe edema, and hyperlipidemia and lipiduria (lipids in the urine).
Asymptomatic hematuria or proteinuria, or a combination of these two, is usually a manifestation of subtle or mild glomerular abnormalities.

Acute kidney injury (previously called acute renal failure) is characterized by rapid decline in GFR (within hours to days) with concurrent dysregulation of fluid and electrolyte balance, and retention of metabolic waste products normally excreted by the kidney including urea and creatinine. In its most severe forms, it is manifested by oliguria or anuria (reduced or no urine flow). It can result from glomerular, interstitial, vascular, or acute tubular injury (ATI).

Chronic kidney disease (previously called chronic renal failure) is defined by a diminished GFR that is persistently less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m⁻ for at least 3 months and/or persistent albuminuria. It may present with a clinically silent decline in renal excretory function in milder forms or with prolonged symptoms and signs of uremia in more severe cases. Chronic kidney disease is estimated to affect 11% of adults in the United States and is particularly common in those greater than 60 years of age. It is the end result of a variety of renal diseases, most commonly diabetic and vascular kidney disease, and is the major cause of death from renal disease. Chronic kidney disease causes significant systemic abnormalities (Table 20.1).
In end-stage kidney disease, the GFR is less than 5% of normal; this is the terminal stage of uremia.

Renal tubular defects are dominated by polyuria (excessive urine formation), nocturia, and electrolyte disorders (e.g., metabolic acidosis). They are the result of diseases that either directly affect tubular structures (e.g., nephronophthisis) or cause defects in specific tubular functions. The latter can be inherited (e.g., familial nephrogenic diabetes, cystinuria, renal tubular acidosis) or acquired (e.g., lead nephropathy).

Urinary tract obstruction and renal tumors have varied clinical manifestations based on the anatomic location and nature of the lesion. Urinary tract infection is characterized by bacteriuria and pyuria (bacteria and leukocytes in the urine). The infection may be symptomatic or asymptomatic, and it may affect the kidney (**pyelonephritis**) or the bladder (cystitis).
**Nephrolithiasis** (renal stones) is manifested by spasms of severe pain (renal colic) and hematuria, often with recurrent stone formation.

Kidney injury that results in azotemia can be either acute or chronic. **Acute kidney injury** can be reversible or progress to **chronic kidney disease**, which is generally irreversible.

One major manifestation of kidney injury is the **nephrotic syndrome**, in which injury to the glomerulus results in abnormal filtration, leading to heavy proteinuria, edema, and metabolic disturbances.
Nephritic syndromes are those in which hematuria, azotemia, hypertension, and subnephrotic proteinuria are the major manifestations.

Diseases involving the tubules and interstitium may have clinical manifestations of the nephritic syndrome, specific defects in tubular function, or acute or chronic kidney disease without specific defining features.
GLOMERULAR DISEASES

Glomerular diseases constitute some of the major problems in nephrology. Glomeruli may be injured by a variety of factors and in the course of several systemic diseases. Disorders in which the kidney is the only or predominant organ involved, such as minimal change disease or membranous nephropathy, constitute the various types of primary glomerulonephritis or, because some do not have a cellular inflammatory component, primary glomerulopathy. Systemic immunologic diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), vascular disorders such as thrombotic angiopathies, metabolic diseases such as diabetes mellitus, and some hereditary conditions such as Fabry disease often affect the glomerulus as one manifestation. These are termed secondary glomerular diseases. However, both the clinical manifestations and glomerular histologic changes in primary and secondary forms can be similar.

In the following sections, we discuss the normal glomerulus and mechanisms of glomerular injury, and then the various primary glomerular diseases. We also briefly review the secondary forms covered in other parts of this book. Table 20.2 lists the most common forms of glomerulonephritis that have reasonably well-defined pathologic and clinical characteristics. The clinical manifestations of glomerular diseases are clustered into the five major groups summarized in Table 20.3. Both primary glomerular diseases and systemic diseases affecting the glomerulus can result in these syndromes. Because glomerular diseases are often associated with systemic disorders, including diabetes, SLE, vasculitis, and monoclonal paraproteinemias, in any patient with manifestations of glomerular disease, it is essential to consider these systemic conditions.
Structure of the Glomerulus

Many clinical manifestations of glomerular diseases result from perturbations of specific components of the glomerulus, so before discussing these diseases we describe the key anatomic structures of glomeruli. The glomerulus consists of an anastomosing network of capillaries lined by fenestrated endothelium invested by two layers of epithelial cells (Fig. 20.1). The visceral epithelial cells, or podocytes, are incorporated into and become an intrinsic part of the capillary wall, separated from endothelial cells by a common basement membrane. The parietal epithelium, located on the inner aspect of Bowman capsule, lines the urinary space, the cavity in which plasma filtrate first collects.

The glomerular capillary wall is the filtration barrier, and consists of the following (Fig. 20.2):
A thin layer of fenestrated endothelial cells, with each fenestra being about 70 to 100 nm in diameter.
The glomerular basement membrane (GBM) with a thick electron-dense central layer, the lamina densa, and thinner electron-lucent peripheral layers, the lamina rara interna and lamina rara externa.

The GBM consists of collagen (mostly type IV), laminin, polyan-ionic proteoglycans (mostly heparan sulfate), fibronectin, entactin, and several other glycoproteins. Type IV collagen forms a network to which other glycoproteins attach. The building block (monomer) of this network is a triple-helical molecule composed of one or more of six types of a chains (COL4A1 to COL4A6). Each molecule consists of an N-terminal domain, a triple-helical domain in the middle, and a globular noncollagenous (NC1) domain at the C terminus. The biochemical properties of these structural components are critical to understanding glomerular diseases. For example, antigens in the NC1 domain are the targets of antibodies in anti-GBM nephritis; genetic defects in the α-chains underlie some forms of Alport syndrome; and the proteoglycan content of the GBM may contribute to its permeability characteristics (Fig. 20.3).

The visceral epithelial cells (podocytes) form interdigitating processes and are adherent to the lamina rara externa of the basement membrane (see Fig. 20.1). Adjacent foot processes are separated by 20- to 30-nm–wide filtration slits, which are bridged by a unique cell-cell junction, the slit diaphragm (see Fig. 20.2).

The entire glomerular tuft is supported by the mesangium, the tissue that lies between the capillaries and is composed of basement membrane–like mesangial matrix that forms a meshwork in which the mesangial cells are embedded (see Fig. 20.1). These cells, of mesenchymal origin, are contractile, phagocytic, and capable of proliferation, of both matrix and collagen production, and of secreting several biologically active mediators. Biologically, they are most akin to vascular smooth muscle cells and pericytes. Because no basement membrane separates mesangial cells from the capillary loops, glomerulonephritides often affect both the mesangial and the intracapillary compartments.

The normal glomerulus is highly permeable to water and small solutes because of the fenestrated nature of the endothelium, and it is impermeable to proteins of the size of albumin (,3.6-nm radius; 70 kilodaltons [kD] molecular weight) or larger. The permeability characteristics of the glomerular filtration barrier allow discrimina-tion among various protein molecules, depending on their size (the larger, the less permeable) and charge (the more cationic, the more permeable). This size- and charge-dependent barrier function is accounted for by the structure of the capillary wall. The charge-dependent restriction is important in the virtually complete exclusion of albumin from the filtrate, because albumin is an anionic molecule.

The podocytes are important for the maintenance of glomerular barrier function and are largely responsible, under normal circumstances, for synthesis of GBM components. Their specialized junctional complex, the slit diaphragm, represents a size-selective distal barrier to the filtration of proteins, enabling effective charge- and size-dependent retention of plasma proteins. Proteins forming the slit diaphragm itself and molecules that are part of the intracellular aspect of the slit diaphragm complex are illustrated in Fig. 20.4. Nephrin is a transmembrane protein with a large extracellular portion composed of immunoglobulin (Ig)-like domains. Nephrin molecules extend toward each other from neighboring foot processes and dimerize across the filtration slit.

Within the cytoplasm of the foot processes, nephrin forms molecular connections with intracellular slit diaphragm components such as podocin and CD2-associated protein (CD2AP), and ultimately links with the actin cytoskeleton, which anchors on focal adhesion hubs.

The importance of the slit diaphragm proteins in maintaining glomerular barrier function is demonstrated by the observation that mutations in the genes encoding them give rise to defects in permeability and familial nephrotic syndromes (discussed later).

Proliferation of mesangial or endothelial cells.
Infiltration of leukocytes, including neutrophils, monocytes, and, in some diseases, lymphocytes.

Basement Membrane Thickening

By light microscopy, this change appears as thickening of the capillary walls, best seen in sections stained with periodic acid–Schiff (PAS). By electron microscopy, such thickening takes one of several forms:

Deposition of amorphous electron-dense material, most often immune complexes, on the endothelial or epithelial side of the basement membrane or within the GBM itself. Fibrin, amyloid, cryoglobulins, and abnormal fibrillary proteins may also deposit in the GBM.
Increased synthesis of the protein components of the basement membrane, as occurs in diabetic glomerulosclerosis.

Formation of additional layers of basement membrane matrices (“double contours”), which most often occupy subendothelial locations and may range from loosely organized matrix to fully duplicated lamina densa, as occurs in the membranoproliferative pattern of glomerular injury, either following episodic **endothelial injury** in the context of subendothelial deposits or in chronic thrombotic microangiopathies.

Mutations in genes encoding components of the GBM sometimes result in thickening, such as in **Alport syndrome**, in which mutations affecting type IV collagen impart a thickened basket-weave appearance to the GBM.
Hyalinosis and Sclerosis
Hyalinosis, as applied to the glomerulus, denotes the accumulation of material that is homogeneous and eosinophilic by light microscopy.

Hyaline is an extracellular, amorphous material composed of high molecular weight plasma proteins that have leaked from the circulation into glomerular structures. When extensive, these deposits may obliterate the capillary lumens of the glomerular tuft. Hyalinosis can be a consequence of endothelial or capillary wall injury, and also occurs following extensive podocyte loss in **diabetic nephropathy** and collapsing glomerulosclerosis. It often is the end result of various forms of glomerular filter damage.

Sclerosis is characterized by deposition of extracellular collagenous matrix. It may be confined to mesangial areas, as is often the case in diabetic glomerulosclerosis, involve the capillary loops, or both. The sclerosing process may also result in obliteration of some (segmental sclerosis) or all (global sclerosis) of the capillary lumens in affected glomeruli.
Many primary glomerulopathies are classified by their histology.

The histologic changes can be further subdivided by their distribution into the following categories: diffuse, involving all of the glomeruli in the kidney; global, involving the entirety of individual glomeruli; focal, involving only a fraction of the glomeruli in the kidney; segmental, affecting a part of each glomerulus; and capillary loop or mesangial, affecting predominantly capillary or mesangial regions.
Glomerular Injury

The GBM is composed of type IV collagen molecules and other matrix proteins. These proteins can be the target of antibodies in some types of **glomerulonephritis**; genetic abnormalities in their composition are the basis for some forms of **Alport syndrome**.

Visceral epithelial cells (podocytes) are a critical component of the glomerular filtration barrier, and their injury leads to leakage of plasma proteins, mainly albumin, into the urinary space (proteinuria).
The acute glomerular response to injury includes hypercellularity with proliferation of mesangial and/or endothelial cells, influx of leukocytes, and, when severe, formation of crescents.
Chronic glomerular responses to injury include basement membrane thickening, hyalinosis, and sclerosis.
Pathogenesis of Glomerular Injury

Immune mechanisms underlie most forms of primary glomerulopathies and many secondary glomerular disorders (Table 20.4). Glomerulonephritis can be induced experimentally by antigen-antibody reactions. Furthermore, glomerular deposits of immunoglobulins, often with components of complement, are found in most individuals with glomerulonephritis. Cell-mediated immune reactions may also play a role, usually in concert with antibody-mediated mechanisms. We begin this discussion with a review of antibody-instigated injury. Two forms of antibody-mediated injury have been established: (1) injury by antibodies reacting *in situ* within the glomerulus, either binding to insoluble fixed (intrinsic) glomerular antigens or extrinsic molecules planted within the glomerulus, leading to deposition and/or

Diseases Caused by In Situ Formation of Immune Complexes

In this form of injury, immune complexes are formed locally by antibodies that react with intrinsic tissue antigens or with extrinsic antigens “planted” in the glomerulus from the circulation (Fig. 20.5A). **Membranous nephropathy** is the classic example of glomerular injury resulting from local formation of immune complexes by antibodies reactive with endogenous antigens. The target antigens are spatially separated in the GBM and not continuous.
The pattern of deposition of antibodies and complement proteins by immunofluorescence microscopy is granular, reflecting localized accumulation of antigen-antibody complexes (Fig. 20.5D).

On electron microscopy, the glomerulopathy is characterized by the presence of numerous discrete subepithelial electron-dense immune complex deposits. These subepithelial deposits, with resultant host responses, eventually result in a thickened basement membrane appearance by light microscopy; hence the term membranous nephropathy.

Some antibodies that bind to intrinsic antigens directly interfere with the function of glomerular proteins. An example are autoantibodies described in **minimal change disease**, which bind to the slit diaphragm component nephrin and disrupt the junctional complexes between podocytes. These antibody-antigen complexes appear to be short lived; as a result, they can be difficult to detect by immunostaining. Antibodies can also react *in situ* with antigens that are not normally present in the glomerulus but are “planted” there. Such antigens may localize to the kidney by interacting with various intrinsic components of the glomerulus. Planted antigens include cationic molecules that bind to anionic components of the glomerulus; DNA, nucleosomes, and other nuclear proteins, which may have an affinity for GBM components; bacterial products; large aggregated proteins (e.g., aggregated immunoglobulins), which deposit in the mesangium due to their size and biochemical properties; and immune complexes themselves, because they continue to have reactive sites for further interactions with free antibody, free antigen, or complement. There is no dearth of other possible planted antigens, including viral, bacterial, and parasitic products and drugs.

Components of the Glomerular Basement Membrane

In anti-GBM antibody–induced glomerulonephritis, antibodies bind to intrinsic antigens distributed along the entire length of the GBM, resulting in a diffuse linear pattern of staining for the antibodies by immunofluorescence techniques (Fig. 20.5B,E). This contrasts with the granular pattern of immunofluorescence staining corresponding to the discrete immune complexes seen in membranous nephropathy, or other glomerular diseases in which large complexes of antigens and antibodies form *in situ*. Although anti-GBM antibody– induced glomerulonephritis accounts for less than 5% of cases of human glomerulonephritis, it is one of the more common causes of the clinical syndrome of RPGN.
Glomerulonephritis Resulting From Deposition of Circulating
Immune Complexes

This type of glomerular injury is caused by the entrapment of circulating antigen-antibody complexes within glomeruli. The antibodies have no immunologic specificity for glomerular constituents, and the complexes localize to the glomeruli because of their physicochemical properties and hemodynamic factors specific to the glomerulus (Fig. 20.5C).

The antigens that trigger the formation of circulating immune complexes may be of endogenous origin, as in the **glomerulonephritis** associated with **SLE** or in **IgA nephropathy**, or they may be exogenous, as may occur in infection-associated glomerulonephritis. Microbial antigens that are implicated include bacterial products (streptococcal proteins), the surface antigen of hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus antigens, and antigens of *Treponema pallidum* and *Plasmodium falciparum*. Some tumor antigens are also thought to cause immune complex–mediated nephritis. In many cases, the inciting antigen is unknown.
Mechanisms of Glomerular Injury Following Immune Complex

Formation The pathogenesis of immune complex diseases is discussed in Chapter 6. Here we briefly review the salient features that relate to glomerular injury. Whatever the antigen may be, antigen-antibody complexes formed or deposited in the glomeruli may elicit a local inflammatory reaction that produces injury. The antibodies may activate complement and engage Fc receptors on leukocytes and perhaps glomerular mesangial or other cells, leading to inflammation. Generally, subendothelial immune complexes provoke leukocyte infiltration and glomerular crescent formation. Similarly, mesangial immune complex deposition can elicit an inflammatory response as the mesangium is not separated from the capillary lumen by a GBM; the glomerular lesions may exhibit leukocytic infiltration and proliferation of mesangial and endothelial cells. In contrast, subepithelial immune complexes are shielded from the circulation by the GBM and do not induce inflammatory responses Electron microscopy reveals electron-dense deposits containing immune complexes that may lie in the mesangium, between the endothelial cells and the GBM (subendothelial deposits), or between the outer surface of the GBM and the podocytes (subepithelial deposits).

Deposits may be located at more than one site in a given case. By immunofluorescence microscopy, the immune complexes are seen as granular deposits along the basement membrane (see Fig. 20.5D), in the mesangium, or in both locations. Once deposited in the kidney, immune complexes may eventually be degraded, mostly by infiltrating neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages, mesangial cells, and endogenous proteases, and the inflammatory reaction may then subside, allowing for complete recovery of the glomerulus. Such a course occurs when the exposure to the inciting antigen is short-lived and/or limited, as in most cases of **poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis**.

However, if immune complexes are deposited repeatedly for prolonged periods, as may be seen with **SLE** or **viral hepatitis**, episodic cellular injury and tissue remodeling results in membranous (subepithelial deposition) or membranoproliferative (subendothelial deposition) patterns of glomerular injury.

Several factors affect the localization of antigen, antibody, or immune complexes in the glomerulus, such as the charge and size of the immune reactants, glomerular hemodynamics, mesangial function, and the integrity of the charge-selective capillary wall barrier, leading to variable patterns of immune-reactant deposition in various forms of **glomerulonephritis** (Fig. 20.6). In turn, the distinct patterns of localization of immune complexes are a key determinant of the injury response and the histologic features that subsequently develop.

In summary, most cases of immune complex–mediated glomerulonephritis are a consequence of deposition of discrete immune complexes, which give rise to granular immunofluorescence staining along the peripheral capillary wall or in the mesangium.

However, it is difficult to determine whether the deposition has occurred *in situ*, by circulating complexes, or by both mechanisms because entrapment of circulating immune complexes can initiate further *in situ* complex formation. Single etiologic agents, such as hepatitis B and C viruses, can cause either a membranous pattern of glomerulonephritis, with subepithelial *in situ* deposition of antigens, or a membranoproliferative pattern indicative of subendothelial deposition of antigens or deposition of circulating complexes.

Activation of Alternative Complement Pathway

Alternative complement pathway activation occurs in the clinicopathologic entity called C3 glomerulopathy, which encompasses the entities of dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis. This is discussed later.
Mediators of Glomerular Injury

Once immune reactants or sensitized T cells have localized in the glomerulus, how does the glomerular damage ensue? The mediators— both cells and molecules—are the usual suspects involved in acute and chronic inflammation, described in Chapter 3, and only a few are highlighted here.
Cells. Numerous recruited and intrinsic cells produce mediators that are responsible for glomerular injury.

Neutrophils and monocytes infiltrate glomeruli in certain types of glomerulonephritis, largely because of activation of complement, resulting in generation of chemotactic molecules (mainly C5a), but also by Fc receptor–mediated activation. Neutrophils release proteases, which cause GBM degradation; oxygen-derived free radicals, which cause cell damage; and arachidonic acid metabolites, which cause vascular changes that contribute to reductions in GFR.
Macrophages and T lymphocytes, which infiltrate glomeruli in antibody- and cell-mediated reactions, release a vast number of biologically active molecules when activated.

**Platelets may aggregate in glomeruli during immune-mediated injury.** Their release of eicosanoids, growth factors, and other mediators may contribute to vascular injury and proliferation of glomerular cells.
Antiplatelet agents have beneficial effects in both human and experimental **glomerulonephritis**.

Resident glomerular cells, particularly mesangial cells, can be stimulated to produce inflammatory mediators, including **reactive oxygen species** (ROS), cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, eicosanoids, nitric oxide, and endothelin. They may initiate inflammatory responses in glomeruli, even in the absence of leukocytic infiltration. Soluble Mediators. Virtually all known inflammatory chemical mediators (Chapter 3) have been implicated in glomerular injury.

Complement activation leads to the generation of chemotactic products that induce leukocyte influx (complement-neutrophil– dependent injury) and the formation of C5b–C9, the **membrane attack complex**. C5b–C9 causes cell lysis and may also stimulate mesangial cells to produce oxidants, proteases, and other mediators. Thus, even in the absence of neutrophils, C5b–C9 can cause proteinuria, as has been demonstrated in experimental membranous glomerulopathy. In some diseases, collectively called C3 glomerulopathies, there is evidence of complement activation resulting from defective regulation of the alternative complement pathway, which can be triggered or exacerbated by the presence of immune complexes or monoclonal immunoglobulins.
Eicosanoids, nitric oxide, angiotensin, and endothelin are involved in hemodynamic changes.

Cytokines, particularly **IL-1** and tumor necrosis factor (**TNF**), which may be produced by infiltrating leukocytes and resident glomerular cells, induce leukocyte adhesion and a variety of other effects.
Chemokines such as monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (also known as CCL2) promote monocyte and lymphocyte influx.

Growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) are involved in mesangial cell proliferation. TGF-β, connective tissue growth factor, and fibroblast growth factor seem to be critical in the extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition and hyalinization leading to glomerulosclerosis in chronic injury. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) maintains endothelial integrity and may help regulate capillary permeability.
The coagulation system is also a mediator of glomerular damage.

Fibrin is frequently present in the glomeruli and Bowman space in glomerulonephritis, indicative of coagulation cascade activation, and activated coagulation factors, particularly thrombin, may be a stimulus for crescent formation.
Epithelial Cell Injury

Podocyte injury is common to many forms of both primary and secondary glomerular diseases, of both immune and nonimmune etiologies. The term podocytopathy has been applied to diseases with different etiologies whose principal manifestation is injury to podocytes. Podocyte injury can be induced by antibodies to podocyte antigens in membranous nephropathy and minimal change disease; by toxins, as in an experimental model of proteinuria induced by puromycin aminonucleoside, which inhibits ribosome function; possibly by certain cytokines; in the context of viral infections such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), parvovirus and SARS-CoV-2; or by unknown circulating factors postulated to underlie some forms of minimal change disease and primary/idiopathic focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). Podocyte injury is reflected by morphologic changes, which include effacement of foot processes, disassembly of the junctional slit diaphragm complex, vacuolization, and Filtration slit Epithelial Effacement Detachment foot Podocytes have a limited capacity for replication and repair, and their loss may be a feature of multiple types of glomerular injury, including FSGS, collapsing glomerulopathy, and diabetic nephropathy. As remaining podocytes undergo compensatory hypertrophy, mild podocyte injury often goes unrecognized in pathologic specimens unless morphometric techniques are applied. In most forms of glomerular injury, loss of slit diaphragms is a key event in the development of proteinuria (see Fig. 20.7). Functional abnormalities of the slit diaphragm may also result from mutations in genes encoding its components, such as nephrin and podocin. Such mutations are implicated in hereditary forms of nephrotic syndrome.

Mechanisms of Progression in Glomerular Diseases

Thus far, the immunologic mechanisms and mediators that initiate glomerular injury have been discussed. The outcome of such injury depends on several factors, including the severity of renal damage, the nature and persistence of the antigens, and the immune status, age, and genetic predisposition of the host.

It has long been known that once any renal disease, glomerular or otherwise, destroys sufficient nephrons to reduce the GFR to about 30% to 50% of normal, progression to end-stage kidney disease proceeds at a steady rate, independent of the original insult or activity of the underlying disease. The secondary factors that lead to progression are of great clinical interest because they are potential targets of therapy that could delay or prevent the inexorable journey to dialysis or transplantation.
The two major histologic characteristics of such progressive renal damage are glomerulosclerosis and tubulointerstitial fibrosis.

Glomerulosclerosis. Sclerosis involving portions of some glomeruli (also referred to as FSGS) develops after many types of renal injury and can lead to proteinuria and increasing functional impairment.

Glomerulosclerosis may be seen even in cases in which the primary disease was nonglomerular. The mechanisms of glomerulosclerosis in this setting are described in the discussion of FSGS later in this chapter. Tubular Injury and Interstitial Fibrosis. Tubulointerstitial injury, manifested by tubular damage and interstitial inflammation, is a component of many acute and chronic glomerulonephritides. Tubulointerstitial fibrosis contributes to progression in both immune and nonimmune glomerular diseases, for example, diabetic nephropathy.

Indeed, the extent of tubulointerstitial damage often shows better correlation with decline in renal function than the severity of glomerular injury. Many factors may lead to such tubulointerstitial injury, including **ischemia** of tubular segments downstream from sclerotic glomeruli, acute and **chronic inflammation** in the adjacent interstitium, and reduced peritubular capillary blood supply. It appears that proteinuria can also cause direct injury to and activation of tubular cells. Activated tubular cells in turn express adhesion molecules and elaborate proinflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors that contribute to interstitial **fibrosis**. Filtered proteins that may produce these tubular effects include cytokines, complement products, the iron in hemoglobin, immunoglobulins, lipid moieties, and oxidized plasma proteins.
Pathogenesis of Glomerular Injury and Progression of Glomerular Disease
Antibody-mediated injury is an important mechanism of glomerular damage, mainly via complement- and leukocyte-mediated pathways. Antibodies may also be directly cytotoxic to glomerular cells.

The most common forms of antibody-mediated **glomerulonephritis** are caused by the formation and accumulation of immune complexes, which may involve either endogenous antigens (e.g., PLA₂R in **membranous nephropathy**) or exogenous antigens (e.g., microbial). Immune complexes show a granular pattern of deposition by immunofluorescence.

Binding of antibodies to intrinsic glomerular proteins can also directly lead to glomerular dysfunction (e.g., nephrin in minimal change disease). In some cases, immune complexes are small and short-lived and may not be readily detectable by immunofluorescence.
Autoantibodies against components of the GBM are the cause of anti- GBM antibody–mediated disease, often associated with severe injury.
The immunofluorescence pattern of antibody deposition is linear.
Activation of the alternative complement pathway is an important mechanism of injury in C3 glomerulopathy that includes dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis.
Soluble inflammatory mediators, such as cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, eicosanoids, nitric oxide, and activated coagulation factors, also contribute to the glomerular injury.
Epithelial cell (podocyte) injury induced by antibodies, toxins, cytokines, infections, and poorly characterized circulating factors is a common manifestation of various forms of glomerular diseases.

Progressive glomerular injury, resulting from either primary or secondary causes, ensues from a cycle of glomerular and nephron loss with compensatory changes, which lead to further glomerular injury, glomerulosclerosis, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and eventually end-stage kidney disease.

Nephritic Syndrome
Glomerular diseases presenting with a nephritic syndrome are characterized by inflammation in the glomeruli. The main clinical features of nephritic syndrome include:
Hematuria (red blood cells and red cell casts in urine)
Proteinuria (usually subnephrotic range) with or without edema
Azotemia

Hypertension Nephritic syndrome is the typical clinical presentation of most proliferative types of glomerulonephritis (GN) such as postinfectious GN, rapidly progressive (crescentic) GN, and proliferative lupus GN (described later, since it also causes nephrotic syndrome).

The lesions that cause the nephritic syndrome have in common proliferation of the cells within the glomeruli, often accompanied by infiltration of inflammatory leukocytes. This inflammatory reaction severely injures the capillary walls, permitting blood to pass into the urine and inducing hemodynamic changes that lead to a reduction in GFR. The reduced GFR is manifested clinically by oliguria, fluid retention, and azotemia. Hypertension probably is a result of both the fluid retention and renin release from the ischemic kidneys. Postinfectious GN is caused by deposition or formation of immune complexes containing microbial antigens, which induce infiltration of leukocytes and proliferation of glomerular cells.

The most common underlying infections are streptococcal, but the disorder may also be associated with other infections. Poststreptococcal GN is decreasing in frequency in the United States due to early antibiotic treatment but continues to be a fairly common disorder worldwide. It usually appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal infection of the pharynx or skin (impetigo). Skin infections are commonly associated with overcrowding and poor hygiene. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis occurs most frequently in children 6 to 10 years of age, but children and adults of any age can be affected.
Pathogenesis

Poststreptococcal GN is caused by immune complexes containing streptococcal antigens and specific antibodies. Only certain strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci are nephritogenic, more than 90% of cases being traced to types 1, 4, and 12, which can be identified by typing of the M protein of the bacterial cell walls.

Serum complement levels are low, compatible with activation of the complement system and consumption of complement components. Clinical Features

In the typical case, a young child abruptly develops malaise, fever, nausea, oliguria, and hematuria (smoky or cola-colored urine) 1 to 2 weeks after recovery from a sore throat. The patients have dysmorphic red cells or red cell casts in the urine, mild proteinuria (usually less than 1 g/day), periorbital **edema**, and mild to moderate hypertension. In adults the onset is more likely to be atypical, such as the sudden appearance of hypertension or edema, frequently with elevation of BUN. The **glomerulonephritis** is subclinical in some infected individuals, and is discovered only on screening for microscopic hematuria carried out during epidemic outbreaks. Important laboratory findings include elevations of antistreptococcal antibody titers and a decline in the serum concentration of C3 and other components of the complement cascade.

More than 95% of affected children eventually recover renal function with conservative therapy aimed at maintaining sodium and water balance. A small minority of children (perhaps less than 1%) do not improve, become severely oliguric, and develop a rapidly progressive form of glomerulonephritis (described later). Some of the remaining patients undergo slow progression to chronic glomerulonephritis with or without recurrence of an active nephritic picture. Prolonged and persistent heavy proteinuria and abnormal GFR mark patients with an unfavorable prognosis.

In adults, the disease is less benign. Although the overall prognosis in epidemics is good, in only about 60% of sporadic cases do the patients recover promptly. In the remainder, the glomerular lesions fail to resolve quickly, as manifested by persistent proteinuria, hematuria, and hypertension. In some of these patients, the lesions eventually clear, but others develop chronic glomerulonephritis or even RPGN.
Rapidly Progressive (Crescentic) Glomerulonephritis

**Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis** (RPGN) is a clinical syndrome associated with severe glomerular injury. It is characterized by relatively rapid and progressive loss of renal function associated with severe oliguria and signs of **nephritic syndrome**. The most common histologic picture is the presence of crescents in most of the glomeruli, hence the name crescentic glomerulonephritis. As discussed earlier, crescents are produced predominantly by the proliferation of the epithelial cells lining the Bowman capsule. The presence of fibrous (healed) crescents indicates that the injury has been present for some time or is episodic; this presentation is often associated with slower disease progression.

Pathogenesis

RPGN, typically associated with crescent formation, may be a manifestation of several different diseases, some restricted to the kidney and others systemic. Although no single mechanism can explain all cases, there is little doubt that in most cases the glomerular injury is immunologically mediated. A practical classification divides crescentic GN into several groups based on immunologic findings (Table 20.6), which have been described as:

Anti-GBM antibody–mediated disease, characterized by linear deposits of IgG and, in many cases, C3 in the GBM. In some of these patients, the anti-GBM antibodies cross-react with pulmonary alveolar basement membranes to produce the clinical picture of pulmonary **hemorrhage** associated with renal failure (**Goodpasture syndrome**). Plasmapheresis to remove the pathogenic circulating antibodies is the mainstay of treatment, which also includes therapy to suppress the underlying immune response.
The antigen common to the alveoli and GBM is a peptide within the noncollagenous portion of the a₃ chain of collagen type IV.
What triggers the formation of these autoantibodies is unclear.

Exposure to viruses or hydrocarbon solvents (found in paints and dyes) has been implicated in some patients, as have various drugs and cancers. There is a high prevalence of certain human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles (e.g., HLA-DRB1) in affected patients, a finding consistent with a genetic predisposition to **autoimmunity**.

Diseases caused by immune complex deposition, with granular deposits of antibodies and complement by immunofluorescence. Crescentic GN can be a complication of any of the immune complex nephritides, including postinfectious **glomerulonephritis**, lupus nephritis, **IgA nephropathy**, fibrillary GN and IgA vasculitis/Henoch-Schönlein purpura. These patients usually cannot be helped by plasmapheresis, and they require treatment for the underlying disease.

Most patients with this type of crescentic GN have circulating antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs) that produce a cytoplasmic (PR3-ANCA) or perinuclear (MPO-ANCA) staining pattern and are known to play a role in some vasculitides (Chapter 11). This type of crescentic GN may be a component of a systemic vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly called Wegener granulomatosis) or microscopic polyangiitis. In many cases, however, pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis is limited to the kidneys. More than 90% of cases have PR3-ANCA (previously c-ANCAs, so called because the antibodies are specific for the neutrophil granule protein proteinase-3) or MPO-ANCA (previously p-ANCAs, indicating reactivity with neutrophil myeloperoxidase) in the serum. ANCAs have proved to be invaluable as a highly sensitive diagnostic marker for pauci-immune crescentic GN, but proof of their role as a direct cause has been elusive. Recent evidence of their pathogenic potential has been obtained by studies in mice showing that transferring antibodies against myeloperoxidase (MPO) induces a form of crescentic GN. B-cell targeting therapies therefore have a critical role in treatment of ANCA-associated vasculitides.

To summarize, about one-fifth of patients with crescentic GN have anti-GBM antibody–mediated glomerulonephritis without lung involvement; another one-quarter have immune complex–mediated crescentic glomerulonephritis; and the remainder (which constitute the majority) are of the pauci-immune type.
MORPHOLOGY

The kidneys are enlarged and pale, often with petechial hemorrhages on the cortical surfaces. Depending on the underlying cause, the glomeruli may show focal and segmental necrosis, diffuse or focal endothelial proliferation, and mesangial proliferation. Segmental glomerular fibrinoid necrosis with destruction of tuft segments and distinctive extracapillary crescents (Fig. 20.9A) adjacent to unaffected glomeruli are the features most typical of pauci-immune RPGN. Crescents consist of proliferating glomerular epithelial cells and monocytes and macrophages that have migrated into the urinary space. Neutrophils and lymphocytes may be present. The crescents may obliterate the urinary space and compress the glomerular tuft. Fibrin strands are frequently prominent between the cellular layers in the crescents. By immunofluorescence microscopy, immune complex–mediated cases show granular immune deposits; anti-GBM-mediated cases show linear GBM fluorescence for Ig and complement; C3GN may have glomerular reactivity for C3 only; and pauci-immune cases have little or no deposition of immune reactants. Electron microscopy discloses deposits in those cases due to immune complex deposition or complement dysregulation. Regardless of type, electron microscopy may show ruptures in the GBM, which allows leukocytes, plasma proteins such as coagulation factors and complement, and inflammatory mediators to reach the urinary space, where they trigger crescent formation (Fig. 20.9B). In time, most crescents undergo organization and foci of segmental necrosis resolve as segmental scars (a type of segmental sclerosis), but restoration of normal glomerular architecture may be achieved with early aggressive therapy.

In Goodpasture syndrome, the course may be dominated by recurrent hemoptysis or even life-threatening pulmonary hemorrhage.

Measurement of serum anti-GBM antibodies, antinuclear antibodies and ANCAs, and analysis of complement-regulatory factors are helpful in the diagnosis of specific subtypes. Although milder forms of glomerular injury may subside, the renal involvement is usually progressive over a matter of weeks and culminates in severe oliguria. Recovery of renal function may follow early intensive plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) combined with steroids and cytotoxic agents in **Goodpasture syndrome**. This therapy can reverse both pulmonary **hemorrhage** and renal failure. Other forms of crescentic GN also respond well to steroids and cytotoxic agents. However, despite therapy, many patients eventually require chronic dialysis or transplantation, particularly if the disease is discovered at a late stage.
Nephritic Syndrome
**Nephritic syndrome** is characterized by hematuria, oliguria with azotemia, proteinuria, and hypertension.
The most common causes are immunologically mediated glomerular injury; lesions are characterized by proliferative changes and leukocyte infiltration.

Acute postinfectious **glomerulonephritis** typically occurs after streptococcal infection in children and young adults but may occur following infection with many other organisms; it is caused by deposition of immune complexes, mainly in the subepithelial spaces, with abundant neutrophils and proliferation of glomerular cells. Most affected children recover; the prognosis is worse in adults.
RPGN is a clinical entity with features of nephritic syndrome and rapid loss of renal function.
RPGN (commonly called crescentic GN) is associated with severe glomerular injury with **fibrinoid necrosis**, GBM breaks, and subsequent proliferation of parietal epithelial cells forming crescents.

Crescentic GN may be mediated by autoantibodies to the GBM or result from immune complex deposition. It can also occur in the absence of significant antibody deposition; most patients with this type of crescentic GN have ANCA-associated vasculitis with circulating ANCAs.
Nephrotic Syndrome

Certain glomerular diseases virtually always produce the nephrotic syndrome. In addition, many other forms of primary and secondary glomerulopathies discussed in this chapter may underlie the syndrome. Before the major diseases associated with nephrotic syndrome are presented, the causes and pathophysiology of this clinical complex are briefly discussed.
Pathophysiology
Nephrotic syndrome is caused by a derangement in glomerular capillary walls resulting in increased permeability to plasma proteins. The manifestations of the syndrome include:
Massive proteinuria, with the daily loss of 3.5 g or more of protein (less in children)
Hypoalbuminemia, with plasma albumin levels less than 3 g/dL
Generalized edema

Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria The various components of nephrotic syndrome bear a logical relationship to one another. The glomerular capillary wall, composed of the endothelium, GBM and podocytes, acts as a size and charge barrier through which the plasma filtrate passes. Increased permeability resulting from either structural or physicochemical alterations in this barrier allows proteins to escape from the plasma into the urinary space, resulting in proteinuria. Heavy proteinuria depletes serum albumin levels at a rate beyond the compensatory synthetic capacity of the liver, resulting in hypoalbuminemia. Increased renal catabolism of filtered albumin also contributes to hypoalbuminemia. The generalized edema is a direct consequence of decreased intravascular colloid osmotic pressure because of low plasma albumin. There is also sodium and water retention, which aggravates the edema (Chapter 4). This seems to be due to several factors, including compensatory secretion of aldosterone, mediated by the hypovolemia-enhanced renin secretion; stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system; and a reduction in the secretion of natriuretic factors such as atrial natriuretic peptides. Edema is characteristically soft and pitting, and is most marked in the periorbital regions and dependent portions of the body. If severe, hypoalbuminemia may also lead to pleural effusions and ascites. The largest proportion of protein lost in the urine is albumin, but globulins are also excreted in some diseases. The ratio of low to high molecular weight proteins in the urine in various cases of nephrotic syndrome is a manifestation of the selectivity of proteinuria. A highly selective proteinuria consists mostly of low-molecular-weight proteins (albumin, transferrin), whereas a poorly selective proteinuria consists of higher-molecular-weight globulins in addition to albumin.

The genesis of hyperlipidemia is complex. Most patients with **nephrotic syndrome** have increased blood levels of cholesterol, triglyceride, very-low-density lipoprotein, low-density lipoprotein, lipoprotein(a), and apoprotein, and there is a decrease in high-density lipoprotein concentration in some patients. These alterations seem to be due to a combination of increased synthesis of lipoproteins in the liver, abnormal transport of circulating lipid particles, and decreased lipid catabolism. Lipiduria follows hyperlipidemia, because lipoproteins also leak across the glomerular capillary wall. The lipid appears in the urine either as free fat or as oval fat bodies, representing lipoprotein resorbed by tubular epithelial cells and then shed along with injured tubular cells that have detached from the basement membrane.

Nephrotic patients are particularly vulnerable to infection, especially staphylococcal and pneumococcal infections, probably due to loss of immunoglobulins in the urine. Thrombotic and thromboembolic complications are also common in nephrotic syndrome, due in part to loss of endogenous anticoagulants (e.g., antithrombin III) in the urine. Renal vein **thrombosis**, once thought to be a cause of nephrotic syndrome, is most often a consequence of this hypercoagulable state, particularly in patients with **membranous nephropathy** (see later).
Pathogenesis

The incidences of the several causes of nephrotic syndrome vary according to age and geography. In children younger than 17 years in North America, for example, nephrotic syndrome is almost always caused by a lesion primary to the kidney; among adults, in contrast, it is often associated with a systemic disease. Pathogenesis

Membranous nephropathy (MN) is a form of chronic immune complex–mediated disease, in which the inciting antigens can sometimes be identified in the immune complexes. The antigens may be endogenous or exogenous. The endogenous antigens may be renal or nonrenal (described later). Exogenous antigens include those derived from hepatitis B virus and *Treponema pallidum* in patients infected with these microbes. complement activation and then shedding of the immune aggregates from the cell surface to form characteristic deposits of immune complexes along the subepithelial aspect of the basement membrane (see (THSD7A), exostocin 1/2 (EXT1/2), neural cell adhesion molecule 1 (NCAM1) or neutral endopeptidase (CD10), a membrane protein recognized by placentally transferred maternal antibodies in cases of neonatal membranous nephropathy. The identification of the most common target antigens is of diagnostic and prognostic value, as associations with systemic autoimmune disease (exostosin) and malignancy (e.g., NELL1) have been described. A subclass of IgG, IgG4, which differs from other IgG subclasses in being a poor activator of the classical complement pathway, is the principal immunoglobulin deposited in many cases of MN, PLA₂R-associated MN in particular. How IgG4 may be associated with complement activation is not clear.

MORPHOLOGY

By light microscopy, the glomeruli either appear normal in the early stages of the disease or exhibit uniform, diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall (Fig. 20.10A). By electron microscopy, the thickening is seen to be caused by irregular electron-dense deposits containing immune complexes between the basement membrane and the overlying epithelial cells, with effacement of podocyte foot processes (Fig. 20.10B and D). Basement membrane material is laid down between these deposits by the podocytes, appearing as irregular spikes protruding from the GBM. These spikes are best seen by silver stains, which color the basement membrane, but not the deposits, black. In time, these spikes thicken to produce domelike protrusions after the immune complex formation subsides and eventually close over the immune deposits, burying them within a markedly thickened, irregular membrane. Immunofluorescence microscopy demonstrates that the granular deposits contain both immunoglobulins and complement (Fig. 20.10C). Immunostains reveal presence of the relevant target antigens in the deposits in most patients. As the disease advances, segmental sclerosis may occur and glomeruli may become totally sclerosed. The epithelial cells of the proximal tubules contain protein reabsorption droplets, and there may be considerable interstitial mononuclear cell inflammation.
Clinical Features

This disorder usually presents with the insidious onset of **nephrotic syndrome** or, in 15% of patients, with sub-nephrotic proteinuria. Hematuria and mild hypertension are present in 15% to 35% of cases. It is necessary in any patient to first rule out secondary causes of nephrotic syndrome, because treatment of the underlying condition (malignant neoplasm, infection, or **SLE**) or discontinuance of the offending drug can reverse or ameliorate the injury.

The course of the disease is variable but generally indolent. In contrast to **minimal change disease**, described later, the proteinuria is nonselective and usually does not respond well to corticosteroid therapy. Complete or partial remissions may occur in up to 40% of patients, even in some patients without therapy. Progression is associated with increasing sclerosis of glomeruli, rising serum creatinine reflecting renal insufficiency, and development of hypertension. Although proteinuria persists in more than 60% of patients, only about 10% die or progress to renal failure within 10 years, and no more than 40% eventually develop severe **chronic kidney disease** or ESKD. The disease recurs in up to 40% of patients who undergo transplantation for ESKD. Spontaneous remissions and a relatively benign outcome occur more commonly in females and in those with proteinuria in the subnephrotic range.

Because of the variable course of the disease, it has been difficult to evaluate the overall effectiveness of corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive therapy in controlling the proteinuria or progression. B-cell targeted therapeutics appear to be the most effective form of therapy to date. It is thought that serologic typing of circulating antibodies to the various antigens as biomarkers of disease activity may aid in the diagnosis, prognosis, and management of **membranous nephropathy**. Minimal Change Disease (Diffuse Podocytopathy With Minimal Changes)

This disorder is characterized by diffuse effacement of foot processes of podocytes, detectable by electron microscopy, in glomeruli that appear normal by light microscopy. It is the most frequent cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, but it is less common in adults (see Table 20.7). The peak incidence is between 2 and 6 years of age. The disease sometimes follows a respiratory infection or routine prophylactic immunization.
Pathogenesis

Historically, this disease was characterized by absence of immune deposits in the glomerulus, which led to dismissal of antibody-mediated causes. However, recent evidence points to an autoantibody-mediated pathogenesis. The current hypothesis is that a subset of minimal change disease is caused by circulating antibodies directed against nephrin, a transmembrane podocyte protein and essential slit diaphragm component, which cause podocyte injury through interference with nephrin crosslinking. Proteinuria ensues due to the rapid breakdown of the podocyte slit diaphragm accompanied by diffuse podocyte foot process effacement, dramatically altering the permeability and selectivity of the glomerular filter. The ultrastructural changes support a primary podocyte injury (podocytopathy), and studies in animal models also suggest the loss of glomerular polyanions. Thus, defects in the charge barrier may contribute to the proteinuria.
MORPHOLOGY

The glomeruli are normal by light microscopy (Fig. 20.11A). By electron microscopy the GBM appears normal, and no electron-dense deposits are seen. The principal lesion is in the podocytes, which show a uniform, diffuse effacement of foot processes, along with loss of intervening slit diaphragms (Fig. 20.11B). This change, often incorrectly termed “fusion” of foot processes, actually represents simplification of the epithelial cell architecture with flattening, retraction, and swelling of foot processes, which is the result of a collapse of their central actin cytoskeleton. Foot process effacement is also present in other proteinuric states (e.g., membranous glomerulopathy, diabetic nephropathy); however, it usually occurs at later stages of the disease and in the context of significant architectural distortion of the glomerulus. It is only when effacement is associated with normal glomeruli by light microscopy that the diagnosis of minimal change disease can be made. In most patients, these podocyte changes are completely reversible after corticosteroid therapy, concomitant with remission of the proteinuria and disappearance of circulating anti-nephrin antibodies. The cells of the proximal tubules are often laden with lipid and protein, reflecting tubular reabsorption of lipoproteins passing through diseased glomeruli (hence the historical name lipoid nephrosis for this disease). Immunofluorescence studies can be negative, but often show subtle diffuse, global fine granular staining for IgG over the podocytes, in the absence of complement reactivity (Fig. 20.11C). IgG staining typically colocal-izes with clustered nephrin and represents binding of anti-nephrin antibodies in the tissue.
Clinical Features

Despite massive proteinuria, renal function most often remains stable, and there is typically no hypertension or hematuria. The proteinuria usually is highly selective, most of the protein being albumin. A characteristic feature is a dramatic response to corticosteroid therapy. Most children (>90%) with minimal change disease respond rapidly to this treatment. However, proteinuria recurs in a significant proportion of patients, and the disease sometimes becomes steroid-dependent or -resistant, and/or progresses to FSGS (discussed later). Nevertheless, the long-term prognosis for patients is excellent, and even steroid-dependent disease may resolve when children reach puberty. Although adults are slower to respond, their long-term prognosis is also excellent. Steroid-dependent and frequently relapsing disease has been reported to respond well to B-cell depletion therapy.

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis

**FSGS** (both primary and secondary forms) is the most common cause of **nephrotic syndrome** in adults in the United States, particularly in individuals of Hispanic and African descent. The disease is characterized by a primary and diffuse podocytopathy and therefore can be considered in the same spectrum as minimal change disease. In contrast to minimal change disease, primary FSGS, as the name implies, is characterized by sclerosis of only a portion of the capillary tuft of only a subset of glomeruli. Primary FSGS typically manifests clinically by the acute or subacute onset of nephrotic syndrome, but in later stages may be associated with sub-nephrotic proteinuria. Hypertension, microscopic hematuria, and some degree of azotemia are commonly present when the disease is first recognized clinically.

FSGS is a result of podocyte loss in the following settings, each of which is discussed in more detail later:
**Primary or idiopathic:** A primary diffuse podocytopathy

**Viral infections and other toxic injuries:** Podocyte loss in the setting of viral infection (such as **HIV**, SARS-CoV-2), heroin addiction (heroin nephropathy), **sickle cell disease**, or other forms of direct toxic podocyte injury

**Adaptive changes:** Podocyte damage due to the adaptive response to high body mass index, loss of renal tissue (after nephrectomy, unilateral renal agenesis, renal **dysplasia**, or reflux nephropathy), or in advanced stages of any other renal disorder with significant nephron loss (most commonly vascular disease)
Inherited forms of **FSGS**, which are uncommon, are associated with mutations in slit diaphragm– and actin cytoskeleton-associated proteins
**High-risk APOL1 alleles:** Following podocyte loss in patients carrying certain APOL1 alleles

**Secondary:** As a secondary event, reflecting scarring and nephron dropout in cases of focal **glomerulonephritis** (e.g., IgA nephropathy, ANCA-associated vasculitis) So-called idiopathic FSGS, a form of primary podocytopathy, accounts for 10% and 35% of cases of nephrotic syndrome in children and adults, respectively. The clinical signs differ from those of minimal change disease in the following respects: (1) there is a higher incidence of hematuria, reduced GFR, and hypertension; (2) proteinuria is more often nonselective; (3) response to corticosteroid therapy is poor; and (4) there is progression to chronic kidney disease, with at least 50% of patients developing ESKD within 10 years.
Pathogenesis of Primary FSGS

Primary FSGS is marked by the same characteristic diffuse podocyte injury that is seen in minimal change disease (diffuse podocytopathy). However, in primary FSGS, the podocytopathy leads to a degree of podocyte loss that exceeds the ability of the surviving podocytes to compensate. The initiating mechanism likely involves undefined circulating factors and genetically determined defects affecting components of the slit diaphragm. Once areas of the tuft are devoid of covering podocytes, hyalinosis and sclerosis ensue, stemming from entrapment of high molecular weight plasma proteins in hyperpermeable foci, capillary collapse, and increased ECM deposition. The recurrence of massive proteinuria after transplantation, sometimes within 24 hours, with subsequent progression to overt lesions of FSGS, recapitulating the disease in the native kidneys, points to persistence of the causative circulating factor in some patients.

The discovery of a genetic basis for some cases of FSGS and other causes of the nephrotic syndrome has improved the understanding of the pathogenesis of proteinuria in the nephrotic syndrome and has provided new methods for diagnosis and prognosis. Inherited forms of FSGS may be associated with:
The first relevant gene identified, NPHS1, encodes the protein nephrin, a key component of the slit diaphragm (see Fig. 20.4).

Several mutations of the NPHS gene have been identified that give rise to congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type, producing a minimal change disease–like glomerulopathy with extensive foot process effacement.

A distinctive pattern of autosomal recessive FSGS results from mutations in the NPHS2 gene, which encodes the intracellular slit diaphragm associated protein podocin. Mutations in NPHS2 are one cause of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome of childhood onset. Some implicated podocin mutations are relatively common variants and show incomplete penetrance; it is suspected that these variants may increase susceptibility to forms of FSGS that are triggered by acquired factors.

Mutations in the gene encoding the podocyte actin-binding proteins α-actinin 4 (ACTN4) and inverted formin-2 (INF2) underlie some cases of autosomal dominant FSGS, which can be insidious in onset but have a high rate of progression to renal insufficiency.

Mutations in the gene encoding TRPC6 have been found in some families with adult-onset FSGS. This protein is widely expressed, including in podocytes, and the pathogenic mutations may perturb podocyte function by increasing calcium flux in these cells.
What the affected proteins have in common is their localization to the slit diaphragm and to adjacent podocyte cytoskeletal structures.
Their specific functions and interactions are incompletely understood, but they all contribute to the integrity of the glomerular filter.

FSGS Associated With High-Risk Alleles of APOL1. In 2010, it was discovered that two sequence variants (G1/G2 risk alleles) in the apolipoprotein L1 gene (APOL1) are strongly associated with an increased risk of chronic kidney disease and renal failure in individuals of African descent, although the mechanisms underlying this association are not yet completely understood. These sequence variants are remarkable because they appear to convey resistance to trypanosome infection, creating a selective pressure that explains their high prevalence in individuals of African descent. One recent line of evidence suggests a pathogenic role of increased APOL1 expression in podocyte cell death. FSGS in the Setting of Adaptive Changes. Adaptive forms of FSGS occur as a complication of glomerular and nonglomerular diseases leading to structural or functional reduction in renal tissue. Particularly striking examples in which this occurs are reflux nephropathy and unilateral renal agenesis. These may lead to progressive glomerulosclerosis and renal failure. The glomerulosclerosis seems to be initiated by the adaptive change that occurs in the relatively unaffected glomeruli of diseased kidneys. Such a mechanism is suggested by experiments in rats subjected to subtotal nephrectomy. Compensatory hypertrophy of the remaining glomeruli initially maintains renal function in these animals, but proteinuria and segmental glomerulosclerosis soon develop, eventually leading to diffuse global glomerulosclerosis and uremia. The glomerular hypertrophy is associated with hemodynamic changes, including increases in glomerular blood flow, filtration, and transcapillary pressure (glomerular hypertension), and often with systemic hypertension. A similar mechanism underlies the development of hypertrophy and FSGS in obese individuals with relative insufficiency of nephron mass compared to body mass (obesity-related FSGS). **FSGS** in **HIV**-Associated and COVID-19–Associated Nephropathy.

HIV infection can directly or indirectly cause several renal complications, including acute renal failure or acute interstitial nephritis induced by drugs or infection, thrombotic microangiopathies, postinfectious **glomerulonephritis**, and, most commonly, a severe form of the collapsing variant of FSGS, termed HIV-associated nephropathy.

A similar form of collapsing glomerulopathy has also been reported in patients with COVID-19. Both diseases are seen more frequently in people of African ancestry than in individuals of European descent, likely due to the higher prevalence of high-risk APOL1 alleles in those of African descent. With the advent of antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection and widespread vaccination for COVID-19, the incidence of these disorders has fallen sharply.
MORPHOLOGY

By light microscopy, the focal and segmental lesions may involve only a minority of the glomeruli (Fig. 20.13A) and may be missed if the biopsy specimen contains a small number of glomeruli. In the sclerotic segments, there is collapse of capillary loops, increase in matrix deposition, and segmental entrapment of plasma proteins along the capillary wall (hyalinosis), which may become so pronounced as to occlude capillary lumens. Lipid droplets and foamy macrophages are often present (Fig. 20.13B). Glomeruli that do not show segmental lesions usually appear normal by light microscopy but may show increased mesangial matrix. By electron microscopy, both sclerotic and nonsclerotic areas show effacement of foot processes, which is diffuse in primary forms of FSGS during acute **nephrotic syndrome**, and there may also be focal detachment of the epithelial cells and denudation of the underlying GBM. By immunofluorescence microscopy, IgM and C3 may be present in the sclerotic areas and/or in the mesangium. In addition to the focal sclerosis, there may be pronounced hyalinosis and thickening of afferent arterioles, particularly in those forms associated with primary vascular injury. With progression of the disease, increased numbers of glomeruli become involved, and sclerosis spreads within each glomerulus as more podocytes are lost. In time, this leads to total (i.e., global) sclerosis of glomeruli, with pronounced tubular **atrophy** and interstitial fibrosis.

A morphologic variant of FSGS, called collapsing glomerulopathy, is characterized by retraction and/or collapse of the entire glomerular tuft, with or without additional FSGS lesions of the type described earlier (Fig. 20.14). This variant of FSGS is the result of accelerated and abundant podocyte loss, followed by capillary collapse and activation and proliferation of parietal epithelial cells, which will eventually migrate onto the denuded segment(s) of the tuft. Collapsing glomerulopathy can be seen in patients with high-risk APOL1 alleles, in those with vaso-occlusive disease and renal infarction, as a feature of drug-induced podocyte injury (e.g., pamidronate), and as the most characteristic lesion of HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN) and COVID-19-associated nephropathy (COVAN). Other features of HIVAN and COVAN include striking focal cystic dilation of tubule segments, which are filled with proteinaceous material, often accompanied by tubulointerstitial inflammation and **fibrosis**, and tubuloreticular inclusions within endothelial cells detected by electron microscopy. Such inclusions have been shown to be modifications of endoplasmic reticulum induced by high levels of type I interferons, which are seen in these disorders. They are not usually present in idiopathic **FSGS** and therefore may have diagnostic value.
Clinical Features

Spontaneous remission is rare in idiopathic FSGS, and responses to corticosteroid therapy are variable. In general, children have a better prognosis than adults. Progression to renal failure occurs at variable rates. About 20% of patients follow an unusually rapid course, with intractable massive proteinuria ending in renal failure within 2 years. Factors associated with rapid progression include the degree of proteinuria, the degree of renal insufficiency at diagnosis, and histologic subtype (the collapsing variant has an unfavorable course). Recurrences are seen in 25% to 50% of patients receiving kidney transplants.
Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis

MPGN is best considered a pattern of glomerular injury rather than a specific disease. It is caused by deposition of immune complexes containing IgG and complement (previously known as type I MPGN), or overactivation of complement without immune complex deposition (now including C3-dominant glomerulopathies, previously called type II MPGN).

The MPGN pattern is characterized histologically by remodeling and duplication of the GBM and proliferation of glomerular cells (with or without leukocyte infiltration), in the presence of deposits along glomerular capillary walls and in the mesangium. Mesangial proliferation and accumulation of matrix is another feature frequently present; therefore, an older term for this pattern of injury is mesangiocapillary (or mesangioproliferative) **glomerulonephritis**.

The MPGN pattern presents as **nephrotic syndrome** in 10% of cases in both children and young adults. Some patients present only with hematuria or proteinuria in the subnephrotic range, but many others have a combined nephrotic-nephritic picture. MPGN is increasingly recognized to be associated with systemic disorders and various known etiologic agents; therefore, careful and thorough clinical work-up of these patients is required.
Pathogenesis

Immune complex deposition in the glomerulus and activation of both classical and alternative complement pathways are frequent findings. The antigens involved in so-called “idiopathic” MPGN are unknown. In secondary forms of MPGN, described later, they are believed to be proteins derived from infectious agents such as hepatitis C and B viruses.
MORPHOLOGY

The glomeruli are large and hypercellular due to proliferation of cells in the mesangium and the presence of infiltrating leukocytes. The glomeruli have an accentuated “lobular” appearance due to the proliferating mesangial cells, increased mesangial matrix and inflammatory leukocytes in capillary lumens (Fig. 20.15). The GBM is thickened, and often shows a “double-contour” or “tram-track” appearance, especially evident on silver or PAS stains. This is caused by “duplication” of the basement membrane (also commonly referred to as splitting), usually as the result of new basement membrane synthesis in response to subendothelial deposits of immune complexes. Between the duplicated basement membranes, there is inclusion or interposition of cellular elements, which can be of mesangial, endothelial, or leukocytic origin. Such interposition also gives rise to the appearance of “split” basement membranes (Fig. 20.16A). Crescents are present in many cases. Immune complex–mediated (formerly type I) MPGN is characterized by the presence of discrete subendothelial electron-dense deposits. Mesangial and occasional subepithelial deposits may also be present (Fig. 20.16A). By immunofluorescence, IgG and C3 are most commonly deposited in a granular, or less commonly, in a confluent pattern, and early complement components (C1q and C4) are often also present, indicative of an immune complex–mediated pathogenesis.
Clinical Features

Most patients with immune complex–mediated MPGN present in adolescence or as young adults with **nephrotic syndrome** and a nephritic component manifested by hematuria or, more insidiously, as mild proteinuria. Few remissions occur spontaneously in either type, and the disease follows a slowly progressive but unremitting course. Some patients develop numerous crescents and a clinical picture of RPGN. About 50% develop chronic renal failure within 10 years. Treatments with steroids, immunosuppressive agents, and antiplatelet drugs have not proven to be of any benefit and current therapy generally focuses on the underlying disorder.
